quote: Kann man zeigen, dass wenn ein von der Zeit unabhängiges beliebiges Kraftfeld gegeben ist und [-alle-] die Bahnen aller Punkte bei allen [-Pun-] Geschwindigkeiten [-gs-] (unterhalb einer Grenze) geschlossene Curven sind, das Kraftfeld nothwendig eines der beiden von Darboux-Halphen angegebene sein muss
english: Can one show that if an arbitrary time-independent force field is given and the orbits of all points at all velocities (below a bound) are closed curves, then the force field must necessarily be one of the two given by Darboux–Halphen?
topic: Short notes: a remark on curve closure, whether polyhedra can be bent, a Hurwitz extremal problem on polygons, a plan to treat the rotation of a fluid-filled body with Klein's parameters, a question on force fields with only closed orbits (Darboux–Halphen), and the start of a statement on expanding continuous functions in series of rational integral functions.

triage.modern_statement: Take a time-independent force field F(q) in the plane or in space, with motion given by q'' = F(q). Suppose that every trajectory is a closed curve, for every starting point and every initial velocity below some bound. Hilbert asks whether F must then belong to one of the two Darboux–Halphen classes. Those classes were found in 1877 as the answer to Bertrand's question about which position-dependent force fields make every orbit a conic. They are (i) Newtonian inverse-square attraction from a centre, together with all its affine transforms, and (ii) the linear (Hooke) central force q'' = -q, together with all its projective transforms. Put simply, this asks whether Bertrand's 1873 theorem (only inverse-square and Hooke forces give all-closed bounded orbits) still holds when the force is no longer assumed to be central and radially symmetric, with the Darboux–Halphen classes as the expected answer.
triage.answered_by: I found no source that addresses Hilbert's question directly. As literally stated, though, the answer is no, and a standard textbook example shows it. The anisotropic harmonic oscillator with commensurate frequencies, e.g. F(x,y) = -(x, 4y), is time-independent, and all of its orbits are closed (they are Lissajous curves). Most of those orbits are not conics, so this field is in neither Darboux–Halphen class. Superintegrability theory (e.g. Rodríguez–Tempesta 2008) studies commensurate anisotropic oscillators as systems with closed bounded orbits. The positive result exists only for central, radially symmetric fields: Bertrand's theorem (1873). The neighbouring classical problem, Bertrand's 'all orbits are conics' question, may never have been fully solved in the plane (Albouy 2005). The counterexample argument is my own reasoning; no cited source applies it to Hilbert's question.

evidence.claim: Bertrand's question: find every position-dependent force field for which the particle moves on a conic section for any initial condition. Darboux and Halphen found two classes of solutions: Newtonian attraction from a centre plus all its affine transforms, and the linear force q'' = -q from a centre plus all its projective transforms.

Albouy says it is not clear that Bertrand's problem has ever been completely solved. Halphen's argument for centrality is 3-dimensional and does not work in the plane, and a claimed complete solution [Imc] is described as clearly wrong.
Bertrand's theorem: among central-force potentials with bound orbits, only two types of radial potentials make every bound orbit closed.
Anisotropic harmonic oscillators with commensurate frequencies are maximally superintegrable and have closed bounded orbits. They are not central-force systems.
Commensurate frequencies give closed orbits, and the isotropic oscillator is maximally superintegrable.

Darboux (1877) asked which central forces give conic orbits, and found surfaces of revolution, each with a force function, on which all orbits are closed. This is related work on all-orbits-closed systems.

triage.why: The note is a real research question: a version of Bertrand's theorem without the assumption that the force is central. Taken literally, an elementary counterexample answers it negatively. The anisotropic oscillator x'' = -x, y'' = -4y has only closed orbits, at every velocity, yet its orbits are mostly non-conic Lissajous figures, so it lies outside both Darboux–Halphen classes. The positive classification is known only under the central, radially symmetric hypothesis (Bertrand 1873). Confidence is medium for three reasons: no source discusses Hilbert's note itself, the counterexample is my inference from standard facts, and Hilbert may have had a narrower class of fields in mind (central or conic-producing ones). Albouy (2005) notes that even Bertrand's related conic-orbit problem may not be completely solved in the plane. Closed-orbit and superintegrable systems, Bertrand-type theorems on curved spaces, and projective dynamics are all still active research areas. This is not one of Hilbert's 23 published problems or the 24th problem.
